This vignette summarizes the model and the procedure implemented by
`mnlfa_ic()`. The paper describing the method is in preparation.

## The model

For person $i$ with person covariates $x_i = (x_{i1}, \dots, x_{iK})$ (no
intercept; for example gender and centered age) and item $j$ with item
covariates $w_j$ (coded as described below), the probability of a correct
response is a two-parameter logistic model whose item intercepts depend on the
person covariates,

$$
\operatorname{logit} P(y_{ij} = 1 \mid \theta_i)
  = \lambda_j \theta_i + \nu_{0j} + \sum_{c=1}^{K} \nu_{jc}\, x_{ic},
\qquad
\theta_i \sim N\big(x_i^\top \alpha,\ \exp(x_i^\top \omega)\big).
$$

- $\lambda_j$ and $\nu_{0j}$ are the slope and intercept of item $j$ for the
  reference person (all covariates 0, latent mean 0 and variance 1).
- $\alpha$ is **impact** on the latent mean and $\omega$ impact on the latent
  log-variance.
- $\nu_{jc}$ is the **uniform DIF** of item $j$ with respect to person
  covariate $c$. In the default **difficulty form** it is stated as a shift in
  item difficulty, in latent-SD units, with positive values meaning harder:

$$
b_{jc} = -\nu_{jc} / \lambda_j = w_j^\top \gamma_c + \varepsilon_{jc}.
$$

DIF is split into a part explained by the item covariates, with **item-covariate
effects** $\gamma_c$, and item-specific **residual DIF** $\varepsilon_{jc}$.
Slopes do not depend on the covariates (only uniform DIF is modeled).

**Coding of item covariates.** Continuous item covariates are centered at their
mean over items (and standardized by default). Categorical ones are
effect-coded, so each category's effect is relative to the average over
categories. Because the DIF model has no intercept, this coding fixes the point
at which explained DIF is zero; what is not explained there is attributed to
impact or residual DIF.

**The slope-intercept form.** With `form = "slope-intercept"`, DIF is stated in
logits instead, $\nu_{jc} = w_j^\top \gamma_c + \varepsilon_{jc}$ (positive =
easier). Without item covariates the two forms are the same model. With item
covariates they are not: a common item-covariate effect is a common shift in
difficulty in one form and a common shift in logits in the other, and the two
can give different impact estimates.

## Why anchors are usually needed, and what replaces them

The likelihood does not change if a constant $\delta_c$ is added to impact
$\alpha_c$ and subtracted from every item's difficulty DIF $b_{jc}$: a
difference between groups can be described as a difference in the trait or as
every item being harder. Conventional analyses resolve this by declaring some
items DIF-free (anchors). With item covariates there is a second
indeterminacy: only the sum $w_j^\top \gamma_c + \varepsilon_{jc}$ is
determined, not its two parts.

MNLFAic replaces anchors with a **sparsity assumption** on residual DIF: among
all parameter values that fit the data equally well, the true one has the
smallest slope-weighted total residual DIF,

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{J} \lambda_j \,\lvert \varepsilon_{jc} \rvert ,
$$

separately for each person covariate $c$. On the logit scale this is the sum
of absolute residual DIF, so without item covariates it is exactly the
minimal-L1 condition of Chen et al. (2023). Two consequences:

- The assumption applies to each column of the person design separately, so
  the coding of the person covariates (for example, dummy coding of a factor,
  or including a product term) is part of the identifying assumption.
- Roughly, items with residual DIF must be a minority, and with a categorical
  item covariate, roughly a minority within each category. The precise
  condition can be checked for a given pattern of residual DIF; its margin
  $\rho$ must be below 1 (`diagnose()`, `ml1_condition_check()`).

## The three stages

1. **Stage 1: maximum likelihood.** The model is fitted with every item's DIF
   free and one item's DIF fixed at 0 for bookkeeping (chosen automatically
   among well-determined items; the results do not depend on which). Item
   covariates play no role here. Integration over $\theta$ uses adaptive
   Gauss-Hermite quadrature; optimization uses a short EM warm start followed
   by Newton steps with the observed information.
2. **Stage 2: the identification step.** For each person covariate, a weighted
   median regression of the anchored difficulty DIF estimates on an intercept
   and the item covariates, with the slopes as weights, chooses the
   representative that minimizes the criterion above. Its residuals are the
   residual DIF estimates, its coefficients the item-covariate effects, and its
   intercept moves impact to its identified value.
3. **Stage 3: inference.** A parametric bootstrap draws Stage-1 estimates from
   their estimated sampling distribution and passes each draw through Stage 2.
   Because Stage 2 is not a smooth function near the truth (items with no
   residual DIF sit exactly on the fitted plane), the draws are centered at a
   modified estimate in which residual DIF smaller than a threshold
   ($\sqrt{2 \log \log N}$ standard errors) is set to 0 (threshold centering).
   - Intervals are symmetric for impact and item-covariate effects, and
     equal-tailed for residual and total DIF.
   - p-values for residual DIF are computed on the logit scale, and residual
     DIF is flagged by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure across all items and
     person covariates.
   - Categorical item covariates get a joint Wald test per person covariate.

Impact on the latent log-variance is not affected by the indeterminacy and gets
Wald intervals from Stage 1.

## Performance and limitations

In the simulations for the paper, residual-DIF tests held their nominal Type I
error and false discovery rate, and intervals for impact and item-covariate
effects had close to nominal coverage when residual DIF was sparse. The main
limitation is **dense and lopsided residual DIF**: when many items have
residual DIF of the same sign (for example 30% of the items, mostly in one
direction), the Stage-2 estimates are biased and the intervals for
item-covariate effects undercover. The diagnostics in `diagnose()` flag some,
but not all, of these situations.

Other limitations of the current version:

- uniform DIF only (slopes do not depend on covariates);
- one latent dimension and binary items;
- the cluster-robust covariance (`cluster =`) is experimental.

## References

Chen, Y., Li, C., Ouyang, J., & Xu, G. (2023). DIF statistical inference
without knowing anchoring items. *Psychometrika, 88*, 1097-1122. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-023-09930-9>

Fang, Z., & Santos, A. (2019). Inference on directionally differentiable
functions. *The Review of Economic Studies, 86*, 377-412.
